subproblems.title: Lusin's theorem (compact form) for measurable maps from ℝ^P into a second-countable space
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, and let Y be a second-countable topological space with a σ-algebra in which every open set is measurable. Let μ be any measure on ℝ^P = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P) (Borel σ-algebra), let A ⊆ ℝ^P be a measurable set with μ(A) < ∞, let g : ℝ^P → Y be measurable, and let ε ∈ (0, ∞] be an extended nonnegative real with ε ≠ 0. Then there is a compact set K ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ K) < ε such that g is continuous on K (ContinuousOn g K).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) {Y : Type} [TopologicalSpace Y] [SecondCountableTopology Y] [MeasurableSpace Y] [OpensMeasurableSpace Y] (μ : Measure (Euclid P)) (A : Set (Euclid P)) (g : Euclid P → Y) (ε : ℝ≥0∞), Measurable g → MeasurableSet A → μ A ≠ ∞ → ε ≠ 0 → ∃ K : Set (Euclid P), IsCompact K ∧ K ⊆ A ∧ μ (A \ K) < ε ∧ ContinuousOn g K
subproblems.natural_proof:
Reuse note. This child is the comparator-accepted declaration dor_ims_lusin_measurable_continuousOn (DAG node root.density_one_implies_regular-a1.imrep_mass_and_support-a1.lusin_covector-a1.lusin_measurable-a1, status accepted, self-contained candidate commit e4172a7b3e6ff6905ecff6f6d729752746d19ff0). Its frozen type is identical, after whitespace normalisation, to the declaration theorem Submission.dor_ims_lusin_measurable_continuousOn in that commit, and that accepted Lean proof stands. It is listed here because it is the accepted prerequisite (depends_on edge) of the reused child lusin_closed, which uses it on every shell. The complete proof below is the finite-measure Lusin step of step 3 of the supplied proof.

Source. Step 3 of the supplied proof applies Lusin's theorem (Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 1.17, chapter-01.txt lines 346–380) on finite-measure pieces S_j ∩ B. Simon's proof of 1.17 partitions A into the level sets f⁻¹[(j−1)/i, j/i), approximates each of them from inside by closed sets (his 1.15(2)), and then passes to a uniform limit of step functions. Here the target Y is only second countable, not necessarily metrizable, so the uniform-limit step is unavailable. The same inner approximation by closed (here compact) sets is therefore applied to the preimages of the members of a countable basis of Y and to their complements. Relative openness of these preimages then gives continuity directly. For Y = (ℝⁿ)*, the case the parent needs, this replaces the supplied proof's coordinatewise use of 1.17.
Notation: B̄(0, R) is the closed ball; all sets below are Borel.

1. (Budget.) Put ε₀ := min(ε, 1). Then 0 < ε₀ ≤ 1 and ε₀ ≤ ε, because ε ≠ 0.

2. (Inner approximation by compact sets.) Let ν := μ⌞A, i.e. ν(S) = μ(S ∩ A). Then ν is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^P, since ν(ℝ^P) = μ(A) < ∞. Claim: for every Borel set S ⊆ A and every real η > 0 there is a compact F ⊆ S with μ(S ∖ F) < η.
 - Every finite Borel measure on a metric space is weakly regular (Mathlib instance WeaklyRegular.of_pseudoMetrizableSpace_of_isFiniteMeasure). So there is a closed F' ⊆ S with ν(S ∖ F') < η/2 (Mathlib MeasurableSet.exists_isClosed_sdiff_lt).
 - The sets ℝ^P ∖ B̄(0, R), R ∈ ℕ, decrease to ∅ and ν is finite. By continuity from above there is R with ν(ℝ^P ∖ B̄(0, R)) < η/2.
 - F := F' ∩ B̄(0, R) is closed and bounded, hence compact, and F ⊆ S. Since S ∖ F ⊆ (S ∖ F') ∪ (ℝ^P ∖ B̄(0, R)) and S ⊆ A, we get μ(S ∖ F) = ν(S ∖ F) < η/2 + η/2 = η.

3. (Countable basis.) Y is second countable, so it has a countable basis 𝓑 of open sets. Every point of Y lies in a member of 𝓑, and Y is non-empty (it contains g(0)), so 𝓑 ≠ ∅; fix a surjection m ↦ U_m from ℕ onto 𝓑. Each U_m is open, hence measurable in Y, so g⁻¹(U_m) is Borel because g is measurable.

4. (The compact set K.) For m ∈ ℕ put V_m := A ∩ g⁻¹(U_m) and W_m := A ∖ g⁻¹(U_m), Borel subsets of A with A = V_m ∪ W_m. By step 2 choose compact F_m ⊆ V_m and F'_m ⊆ W_m with μ(V_m ∖ F_m) < ε₀·2^(−m−3) and μ(W_m ∖ F'_m) < ε₀·2^(−m−3). Put K := ⋂_{m∈ℕ} (F_m ∪ F'_m).
 (a) K is a closed subset of the compact set F_0 ∪ F'_0, hence compact, and K ⊆ F_0 ∪ F'_0 ⊆ V_0 ∪ W_0 = A.
 (b) Let x ∈ A ∖ K. Then x ∉ F_m ∪ F'_m for some m, and x ∈ V_m or x ∈ W_m, so x ∈ (V_m ∖ F_m) ∪ (W_m ∖ F'_m). By countable subadditivity, μ(A ∖ K) ≤ Σ_m 2·ε₀·2^(−m−3) = ε₀/2 < ε₀ ≤ ε.
 (c) g is continuous on K. Fix m. Since F_m ⊆ g⁻¹(U_m), F'_m ∩ g⁻¹(U_m) = ∅ and K ⊆ F_m ∪ F'_m, we have K ∩ g⁻¹(U_m) = K ∖ F'_m = K ∩ (ℝ^P ∖ F'_m). This set is relatively open in K because F'_m is closed. Every open U ⊆ Y is the union of the members of 𝓑 contained in it, so K ∩ g⁻¹(U) = ⋃_{m : U_m ⊆ U} (K ∩ (ℝ^P ∖ F'_m)) is relatively open in K. Hence the restriction of g to K is continuous, i.e. ContinuousOn g K.

Thus K is a compact subset of A with μ(A ∖ K) < ε on which g is continuous. ∎
proof_key_steps: Restrict μ to A: a finite Borel measure on ℝ^P is weakly regular, and cutting a closed inner approximant with a large closed ball gives compact inner approximants of every Borel S ⊆ A.
For each member U_m of a countable basis of Y choose compact F_m ⊆ A ∩ g⁻¹(U_m) and F'_m ⊆ A ∖ g⁻¹(U_m) with defects ε₀·2^(−m−3); K = ⋂_m (F_m ∪ F'_m) ⊆ A is compact and μ(A ∖ K) ≤ ε₀/2 < ε.
K ∩ g⁻¹(U_m) = K ∖ F'_m is relatively open in K for every m, so g is continuous on K.

subproblems.title: Lusin's theorem for Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n with a closed set, sets of infinite measure allowed (step 2 of Simon's proof of Ch. 2, 1.5)
subproblems.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ and let Y be a second-countable topological space with a σ-algebra containing every open set. Let g : ℝ^n → Y be measurable, where ℝ^n = Euclid n carries its Borel σ-algebra. Let B ⊆ ℝ^n be measurable, possibly with L^n(B) = ∞, and let ε ∈ (0, ∞]. Then there is a closed set C ⊆ B such that g is continuous on C (ContinuousOn g C) and L^n(B ∖ C) < ε, where L^n = volume.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) {Y : Type} [TopologicalSpace Y] [SecondCountableTopology Y] [MeasurableSpace Y] [OpensMeasurableSpace Y] (g : Euclid n → Y) (B : Set (Euclid n)), Measurable g → MeasurableSet B → ∀ ε : ℝ≥0∞, 0 < ε → ∃ C : Set (Euclid n), C ⊆ B ∧ IsClosed C ∧ ContinuousOn g C ∧ volume (B \ C) < ε

Reuse note. This child is the comparator-accepted declaration codim1_rdo_c1a_lusin_isClosed (DAG node root.dimension_reduction_results-a1.codimension_one_regularity-a1.region_density_one-a1.rectifiable_density_one-a1.c1_approximation-a1.lusin_closed-a1, status accepted, candidate commit 1ebfef61050d90da64df918659b2c1fa5df4f610). Its frozen type is identical, after whitespace normalisation, to the declaration theorem Submission.codim1_rdo_c1a_lusin_isClosed in that commit, and that accepted Lean proof stands. Its history contains the accepted sibling lusin_finite (commit e4172a7b), its recorded dependency. The complete proof below is step 3 of the supplied proof.

Source. Step 3 of the supplied proof is Simon's sentence in the proof of Ch. 2, Theorem 1.5: "By Lusin's theorem (which applies to sets of infinite measure for Lⁿ) there is a closed set C ⊆ B such that ∇f|C is continuous" (chapter-02.txt lines 246–250). As in the supplied proof, the infinite-measure case is handled by applying the finite-measure theorem on bounded shells and gluing along a locally finite family. This is Simon's own device for the infinite-measure case of Ch. 1, 1.15(2) (chapter-01.txt lines 323–342), with his sets V_j replaced by shells. On each shell the sibling lusin_finite is used. It allows any second-countable target, so it covers Y = (ℝⁿ)* without the supplied proof's coordinatewise reduction.
Notation: Lⁿ = volume; |·| is the Euclidean norm; B(x, r) is the open ball and B̄(x, r) the closed ball.

1. (Budget.) Put δ := min(ε, 1), so 0 < δ ≤ 1 and δ ≤ ε. For j ∈ ℕ put δ_j := δ·2^(−j−2) > 0. Then Σ_j δ_j = δ/2 < δ ≤ ε; the middle inequality is strict because 0 < δ < ∞.

2. (Shells.) For j ∈ ℕ let S_j := {x ∈ ℝⁿ : j ≤ |x| < j + 1}.
 - S_j is Borel (the preimage of [j, j + 1) under the continuous norm), and S_j ⊆ B̄(0, j + 1), so Lⁿ(S_j) < ∞.
 - The S_j are pairwise disjoint, and every x lies in S_⌊|x|⌋.
 - Every family (F_j)_{j∈ℕ} with F_j ⊆ S_j is locally finite: if y ∈ B(x, 1) ∩ F_j, then j ≤ |y| < |x| + 1, so B(x, 1) meets F_j only for the finitely many j < |x| + 1.

3. (Lusin on each shell.) Fix j. B_j := B ∩ S_j is measurable with Lⁿ(B_j) ≤ Lⁿ(S_j) < ∞, and δ_j ≠ 0. Apply lusin_finite with P = n, the space Y, μ = Lⁿ, A = B_j, the map g and tolerance δ_j. It gives a compact K_j ⊆ B_j with Lⁿ(B_j ∖ K_j) < δ_j such that g is continuous on K_j. K_j is closed, being compact in the Hausdorff space ℝⁿ.

4. (Gluing.) Put C := ⋃_{j∈ℕ} K_j. Then C ⊆ ⋃_j B_j ⊆ B.
 - K_j ⊆ S_j, so the family (K_j) is locally finite by step 2.
 - A locally finite union of closed sets is closed (Mathlib LocallyFinite.isClosed_iUnion), so C is closed.
 - A map that is continuous on each member of a locally finite family of closed sets is continuous on their union (Mathlib LocallyFinite.continuousOn_iUnion): near any point only finitely many K_j occur, and the pasting lemma for finitely many closed sets applies. Hence g is continuous on C.

5. (Measure.) Let x ∈ B ∖ C and j := ⌊|x|⌋. Then x ∈ B ∩ S_j = B_j, and x ∉ K_j because K_j ⊆ C. Hence B ∖ C ⊆ ⋃_j (B_j ∖ K_j), and countable subadditivity with steps 1 and 3 gives
 Lⁿ(B ∖ C) ≤ Σ_j Lⁿ(B_j ∖ K_j) ≤ Σ_j δ_j = δ/2 < δ ≤ ε.

Thus C is a closed subset of B on which g is continuous, with Lⁿ(B ∖ C) < ε. ∎
proof_key_steps: Budget δ = min(ε, 1), δ_j = δ·2^(−j−2), Σ_j δ_j = δ/2 < ε; bounded Borel shells S_j = {j ≤ |x| < j + 1} partition ℝⁿ, and families F_j ⊆ S_j are locally finite.
lusin_finite on B ∩ S_j (finite measure) gives compact K_j ⊆ B ∩ S_j with Lⁿ((B ∩ S_j) ∖ K_j) < δ_j and g continuous on K_j.
C = ⋃_j K_j ⊆ B is closed and g is continuous on C (locally finite closed family); B ∖ C ⊆ ⋃_j ((B ∩ S_j) ∖ K_j) has measure ≤ δ/2 < ε.

subproblems.title: Egoroff's theorem on ℝ^n with a closed good set and uniform convergence on its compact subsets (steps 5–6 of Simon's proof of Ch. 2, 1.5)
subproblems.statement: Let n ∈ ℕ and let C ⊆ ℝ^n = Euclid n be measurable, possibly with L^n(C) = ∞. Notation: Lⁿ = volume; Df(x) := fderiv ℝ f x ∈ (ℝⁿ)*; |·| is the Euclidean norm and ‖·‖ the operator norm.

1. (The remainder.) For x ≠ y put R(x, y) := |f(y) − f(x) − Df(x)(y − x)| / |y − x|.
 (a) Bound. Since f is L-Lipschitz, ‖Df(x)‖ ≤ L for every x ∈ ℝⁿ (Mathlib norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz; where f is not differentiable, Df(x) = 0). Hence 0 ≤ R(x, y) ≤ (|f(y) − f(x)| + ‖Df(x)‖·|y − x|)/|y − x| ≤ 2L.
 (b) Continuity in y. For fixed x, the map y ↦ R(x, y) is continuous on ℝⁿ ∖ {x}: f is continuous (being Lipschitz), Df(x) is a fixed continuous linear functional, and y ↦ |y − x| is continuous and non-zero there.
 (c) Measurability in x. For fixed y, the map x ↦ R(x, y) is Borel on the open set ℝⁿ ∖ {y}.
 - x ↦ Df(x) is Borel on ℝⁿ (Mathlib measurable_fderiv). On C it is even continuous, by hypothesis, but this is not needed.
 - Hence x ↦ (Df(x), y − x) is Borel into (ℝⁿ)* × ℝⁿ. Both factors are second countable, so the Borel σ-algebra of the product is the product σ-algebra.
 - Evaluation (λ, v) ↦ λ(v) is continuous, so x ↦ Df(x)(y − x) is Borel.
 - f is continuous, and x ↦ |y − x| is continuous and non-zero on ℝⁿ ∖ {y}.

2. (A countable dense subset.) ℝⁿ is a separable metric space, so C contains a countable set D with C ⊆ closure(D) (Mathlib IsSeparable.exists_countable_dense_subset).

3. (The suprema ρ_k.) For k ∈ ℕ and x ∈ ℝⁿ put

By 1(a), 0 ≤ ρ_k ≤ 2L.
 (a) ρ_k is Borel. For y ∈ D let φ_{k,y}(x) := R(x, y) if 0 < |y − x| < 1/(k + 1), and φ_{k,y}(x) := 0 otherwise. The set {x : 0 < |y − x| < 1/(k + 1)} is open and contained in ℝⁿ ∖ {y}, so φ_{k,y} is Borel by 1(c). All the values are ≥ 0, so ρ_k = sup_{y∈D} φ_{k,y}; both sides are 0 when no y ∈ D satisfies 0 < |y − x| < 1/(k + 1). A supremum of countably many Borel functions with values in [0, 2L] is Borel.
 (b) Domination on C. If x, y ∈ C and 0 < |y − x| < 1/(k + 1), then R(x, y) ≤ ρ_k(x).
 - Since y ∈ closure(D), there are d_m ∈ D with d_m → y.
 - The set {z : 0 < |z − x| < 1/(k + 1)} is open and contains y, so it contains d_m for all large m. For those m, R(x, d_m) ≤ ρ_k(x).
 - By 1(b), R(x, d_m) → R(x, y). Hence R(x, y) ≤ ρ_k(x).

 (c) Pointwise convergence on C. Let x ∈ C. Since f is differentiable at x with derivative Df(x), for every η > 0 there is r > 0 such that |f(y) − f(x) − Df(x)(y − x)| ≤ η|y − x| whenever |y − x| < r. For k with 1/(k + 1) < r, every term R(x, y) in the definition of ρ_k(x) has |y − x| < r and is therefore ≤ η, so 0 ≤ ρ_k(x) ≤ η. Hence ρ_k(x) → 0 as k → ∞. This is Simon's "lim_{y→x, y∈C} R(x, y) = 0 for all x ∈ C".

4. (Egorov with a closed good set.) C is closed, hence measurable. Apply the sibling egorov_closed with:
 - the set C;
 - the measurable functions η_k := ρ_k (k ∈ ℕ) of 3(a);
 - the measurable limit g ≡ 0, the convergence at every point of C being 3(c);
 - the given ε.
It gives a closed set A ⊆ C with Lⁿ(C ∖ A) < ε such that ρ_k → 0 uniformly on every compact Q ⊆ A.

5. (Whitney's condition 1.6(∗).) Let Q ⊆ A be compact and ε' > 0. By step 4 there is k with |ρ_k(x)| < ε' for all x ∈ Q. Put δ' := 1/(k + 1) > 0, and let x ∈ Q and y ∈ A with |x − y| < δ'.
 - If y = x, then |f(y) − f(x) − Df(x)(y − x)| = |Df(x)(0)| = 0 ≤ ε'·|y − x|.
 - Otherwise 0 < |y − x| < 1/(k + 1) and x, y ∈ A ⊆ C, so 3(b) gives R(x, y) ≤ ρ_k(x) < ε'. Multiplying by |y − x| > 0 gives |f(y) − f(x) − Df(x)(y − x)| ≤ ε'|y − x|.

Simon Ch. 2, Theorem 1.6 (chapter-02.txt lines 173–186) states this theorem but prints no proof: line 186 says "For the proof see for example [EG92] or [Fed69]", and Remark 1.7(2) treats only n = 1. So there is no printed proof to copy. The proof below is the standard Whitney-decomposition argument of [EG92] (Evans–Gariepy, Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions, §6.5). It is given in the form kernel-checked in the SimonGMT files Chapter02/WhitneyCover.lean, WhitneyPartition.lean, WhitneyJet.lean and WhitneyExtension.lean (theorem exists_contDiff_one_extension_of_whitney). Notation: |·| is the Euclidean norm, ‖·‖ the operator norm on (ℝⁿ)*, B(x, r) the open ball, B̄(x, r) the closed ball, and d(x) := dist(x, A).

0. (Trivial case; radius function.) If A = ∅, take g := 0: it is C¹, and the other two conclusions are vacuous. Assume A ≠ ∅, and put r(x) := min(1, d(x))/100.
 - d is 1-Lipschitz, so |r(x) − r(y)| ≤ |x − y|/100.
 - 0 ≤ r ≤ 1/100 and 100·r(x) ≤ d(x).
 - r(x) > 0 exactly when x ∉ A, because A is closed.

1. (Affine jets.) For b ∈ ℝⁿ let P_b(x) := h(b) + D(b)(x − b). P_b is affine, hence C^∞, with derivative D(b) at every point, and P_b(b) = h(b). For all a, b, x,
 P_b(x) − P_a(x) = [h(b) − h(a) − D(a)(b − a)] + (D(b) − D(a))(x − b),
so |P_b(x) − P_a(x)| ≤ |h(b) − h(a) − D(a)(b − a)| + ‖D(b) − D(a)‖·|x − b|.

2. (Local uniform estimate.) Let a ∈ A and η > 0. Then there is δ ∈ (0, 1] such that
 (i) ‖D(b) − D(a)‖ ≤ η for all b ∈ A with |b − a| < δ, and
 (ii) |h(c) − h(b) − D(b)(c − b)| ≤ η|c − b| for all b, c ∈ A with |b − a| < δ and |c − a| < δ.
Proof.
 - Q := A ∩ B̄(a, 1) is compact (closed and bounded in ℝⁿ) and Q ⊆ A, so the hypothesis gives r₀ > 0 for Q and η.
 - Continuity of D on A at a gives η₀ > 0 with ‖D(b) − D(a)‖ < η for all b ∈ A with |b − a| < η₀.
 - Take δ := min(1, η₀, r₀/3). Then (i) holds by the choice of η₀.
 - For (ii): b ∈ Q because |b − a| < δ ≤ 1, and |b − c| < 2δ < r₀. So the hypothesis applies with x = b and y = c.

3. (Nearest points.) A is closed and non-empty and ℝⁿ is proper, so every x has a nearest point π(x) ∈ A, with |x − π(x)| = d(x).
 - For b ∈ A: |π(x) − b| ≤ |π(x) − x| + |x − b| ≤ 2|x − b|.
 - For a ∈ A: π(a) = a.

4. (Whitney balls.) Apply the Vitali covering lemma (Mathlib Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement_ball, τ = 4) to the balls B(x, r(x)), x ∈ ℝⁿ ∖ A, whose radii are ≤ 1/100. It gives a set Z ⊆ ℝⁿ ∖ A of centres such that:
 - the balls B(c, r(c)), c ∈ Z, are pairwise disjoint;
 - for every x ∉ A there is c ∈ Z with B(x, r(x)) ⊆ B(c, 4r(c)); since r(x) > 0, this gives |x − c| < 4r(c).

5. (Comparability and bounded overlap.) For x ∉ A let Z_x := {c ∈ Z : |x − c| ≤ r(x) + 10·r(c)}.
 (a) If c ∈ Z_x, then r(x)/2 ≤ r(c) ≤ 2r(x) and |x − c| ≤ 21·r(x). Indeed |r(x) − r(c)| ≤ |x − c|/100 ≤ (r(x) + 10·r(c))/100. Hence r(c) ≤ r(x) + (r(x) + 10·r(c))/100, i.e. 0.9·r(c) ≤ 1.01·r(x), so r(c) ≤ 2r(x). Also r(x) ≤ r(c) + (r(x) + 10·r(c))/100, i.e. 0.99·r(x) ≤ 1.1·r(c), so r(c) ≥ 0.9·r(x) ≥ r(x)/2. Finally |x − c| ≤ r(x) + 10·r(c) ≤ 21·r(x).
 (b) There is N ∈ ℕ, depending only on n, with #Z_x ≤ N for every x ∉ A.
 - The map c ↦ (c − x)/r(x) is injective and sends Z_x into B̄(0, 21).
 - Distinct c, c' ∈ Z satisfy |c − c'| ≥ r(c). Otherwise c' ∈ B(c, r(c)) ∩ B(c', r(c')), contradicting disjointness.
 - With (a), the images of distinct elements of Z_x are therefore at distance ≥ r(c)/r(x) ≥ 1/2.
 - Fix a finite 1/4-net of the totally bounded set B̄(0, 21), with N points. Assign to each image a net point at distance < 1/4. Two distinct images assigned the same net point would be at distance < 1/2. So the assignment is injective, and #Z_x ≤ N.

6. (Bumps.) Fix ψ ∈ C^∞(ℝⁿ) with 0 ≤ ψ ≤ 1, ψ = 1 on B̄(0, 4) and ψ = 0 outside B(0, 8) (Mathlib ContDiffBump with radii 4 < 8). ψ is C¹ with compact support, hence Λ-Lipschitz for some Λ. For c ∈ Z put φ_c(x) := ψ((x − c)/r(c)). Then:
 - φ_c is C^∞ and 0 ≤ φ_c ≤ 1;
 - φ_c = 1 on B̄(c, 4r(c)) and φ_c = 0 outside B(c, 8r(c));
 - φ_c is (Λ/r(c))-Lipschitz, so ‖Dφ_c(x)‖ ≤ Λ/r(c) for all x.

7. (Local finiteness.) Let x ∉ A and |y − x| < r(x).
 - y ∉ A, since r(x) ≤ d(x)/100 < d(x).
 - If c ∈ Z ∖ Z_x, then |y − c| ≥ |x − c| − |y − x| > 10·r(c) ≥ 8·r(c), so φ_c(y) = 0.
 - Hence on B(x, r(x)) the function S := Σ_{c∈Z} φ_c equals the finite sum Σ_{c∈Z_x} φ_c. So S is C^∞ on the open set ℝⁿ ∖ A.
 - S(x) ≥ 1 for every x ∉ A: by step 4 pick c ∈ Z with |x − c| < 4r(c); then c ∈ Z_x and φ_c(x) = 1.

8. (Partition of unity.) For x ∉ A and c ∈ Z put w_c(x) := φ_c(x)/S(x).
 - Each w_c is C^∞ on ℝⁿ ∖ A, and 0 ≤ w_c ≤ 1.
 - By step 7, Σ_{c∈Z_x} w_c(y) = 1 for |y − x| < r(x). Hence Σ_{c∈Z_x} Dw_c(x) = 0.
 - Dw_c = Dφ_c/S − φ_c·DS/S², with S ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ φ_c ≤ 1. So ‖Dw_c(x)‖ ≤ ‖Dφ_c(x)‖ + ‖DS(x)‖.
 - For c ∈ Z_x, ‖Dφ_c(x)‖ ≤ Λ/r(c) ≤ 2Λ/r(x) by 5(a). Since DS(x) = Σ_{c∈Z_x} Dφ_c(x), we get ‖DS(x)‖ ≤ 2NΛ/r(x).
Therefore Σ_{c∈Z_x} ‖Dw_c(x)‖ ≤ M/r(x), where M := 2Λ(N + 1)² does not depend on x.

9. (The extension.) For c ∈ Z let b_c := π(c) ∈ A. Define g(x) := h(x) for x ∈ A and g(x) := Σ_{c∈Z} w_c(x)·P_{b_c}(x) for x ∉ A. By step 7, near each x ∉ A this is the finite sum Σ_{c∈Z_x} w_c·P_{b_c}. Hence g = h on A, g is C^∞ on ℝⁿ ∖ A, and for x ∉ A
 Dg(x) = Σ_{c∈Z_x} [w_c(x)·D(b_c) + P_{b_c}(x)·Dw_c(x)].

10. (Anchor distances.) Let x ∉ A and c ∈ Z_x.
 - d(c) ≤ d(x) + |x − c|, and |x − c| ≤ 21·r(x) ≤ (21/100)·d(x).
 - So |x − b_c| ≤ |x − c| + d(c) ≤ 2|x − c| + d(x) ≤ 2d(x).
 - Consequently, for a ∈ A, using d(x) ≤ |x − a|: |x − b_c| ≤ 2|x − a| and |b_c − a| ≤ |b_c − x| + |x − a| ≤ 3|x − a|.

11. (Dg = D on A.) Let a ∈ A and ε > 0. Take δ from step 2 with η := ε/5, and let |x − a| < δ/4. We show |g(x) − g(a) − D(a)(x − a)| ≤ ε|x − a|. Since g(a) = h(a), the left side is |g(x) − P_a(x)|.
 - If x ∈ A: by 2(ii) with b = a and c = x, |h(x) − h(a) − D(a)(x − a)| ≤ (ε/5)|x − a|.
 - If x ∉ A: since Σ_{c∈Z_x} w_c(x) = 1, g(x) − P_a(x) = Σ_{c∈Z_x} w_c(x)·(P_{b_c}(x) − P_a(x)).
 - For c ∈ Z_x, step 10 gives |b_c − a| ≤ 3|x − a| < δ and |x − b_c| ≤ 2|x − a|.
 - Step 1 together with step 2 ((ii) for b = a, c = b_c; (i) for b = b_c) gives |P_{b_c}(x) − P_a(x)| ≤ (ε/5)|b_c − a| + (ε/5)|x − b_c| ≤ (ε/5)(3 + 2)|x − a| = ε|x − a|.
 - A convex combination of numbers of absolute value ≤ ε|x − a| has absolute value ≤ ε|x − a|.
Hence g has Fréchet derivative D(a) at a (HasFDerivAt g (D a) a). With step 9, g is differentiable everywhere, Dg = D on A, and Dg is continuous at every point of the open set ℝⁿ ∖ A.

12. (Dg is continuous at points of A.) Let a ∈ A and ε > 0. Put η := ε/(2(1 + 700M)), take δ ∈ (0, 1] from step 2 for this η, and let |x − a| < δ/4.
 - If x ∈ A: by step 11 and 2(i), ‖Dg(x) − Dg(a)‖ = ‖D(x) − D(a)‖ ≤ η ≤ ε/2.
 - If x ∉ A: let b := π(x), so |x − b| = d(x) ≤ |x − a| and |b − a| ≤ 2|x − a| < δ. Since Σ_{c∈Z_x} w_c(x) = 1 and Σ_{c∈Z_x} Dw_c(x) = 0, step 9 gives
 Dg(x) − D(a) = Σ_{c∈Z_x} w_c(x)·(D(b_c) − D(a)) + Σ_{c∈Z_x} (P_{b_c}(x) − P_b(x))·Dw_c(x).
 - First sum: for c ∈ Z_x, |b_c − a| ≤ 3|x − a| < δ, so ‖D(b_c) − D(a)‖ ≤ η by 2(i). Being a convex combination, the first sum has norm ≤ η.
 - Second sum: d(x) ≤ |x − a| < 1/4, so r(x) = d(x)/100. For c ∈ Z_x:
 * |b_c − b| ≤ |b_c − x| + |x − b| ≤ 3d(x);
 * ‖D(b_c) − D(b)‖ ≤ ‖D(b_c) − D(a)‖ + ‖D(b) − D(a)‖ ≤ 2η;
 * |h(b_c) − h(b) − D(b)(b_c − b)| ≤ η|b_c − b| ≤ 3η·d(x), by 2(ii), since b and b_c lie in A within δ of a;
 * |x − b_c| ≤ 2d(x).
 By step 1, |P_{b_c}(x) − P_b(x)| ≤ 3η·d(x) + 2η·2d(x) = 7η·d(x) = 700η·r(x). With step 8, the second sum has norm ≤ 700η·r(x)·M/r(x) = 700Mη.
 Hence ‖Dg(x) − D(a)‖ ≤ η(1 + 700M) = ε/2 < ε.
So Dg is continuous at a.

13. (Conclusion.) By steps 9, 11 and 12, g is differentiable on ℝⁿ with continuous derivative, so g is C¹ (ContDiff ℝ 1 g, via Mathlib contDiff_one_iff_fderiv). By step 9, g = h on A. By step 11, HasFDerivAt g (D a) a for every a ∈ A. The hypothesis that h is continuous on A is not used; it is part of the frozen statement and is harmless. ∎
